analysis.one_liner: Opens local phone markets to competition and loosens broadcast and cable regulation.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 305-117 on August 4, 1995, but the Senate never voted on this House bill and it died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the 1934 Communications Act to force local telephone monopolies to open their networks to competitors, and in exchange let the regional Bell companies into long-distance service and manufacturing once states certify competition. It also lets phone companies sell cable TV, extends broadcast licenses to seven years, relaxes FCC ownership caps, and weakens cable rate oversight. Congress's stated goal was lower prices through competition; the price was softer rules on who can own the media.
analysis.who_benefits: Telephone customers (through mandated network access, number portability, and protection from carrier 'slamming'), new telecom entrants and small businesses (market-entry reviews, a small-business complaint procedure, a development fund), people with disabilities (equipment accessibility rules), parents (V-chip blocking technology), and internet service providers (liability immunity for third-party content). Concentrated interests also gain: Bell companies get long-distance entry, broadcasters get longer licenses and looser ownership caps, and cable operators get lighter rate regulation.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every local phone company to interconnect with competitors, unbundle network elements, offer resale, provide number portability and dialing parity, and negotiate in good faith under state supervision

Supersedes the 1982 court order that broke up the Bell system, creating a statutory path for Bell companies to offer long-distance service once state commissions certify they have opened their local markets
Directs the FCC to bar carriers from switching a customer's phone provider without verification, and makes violators liable for charges collected after an illegal switch (the 'slamming' problem)

Requires that new network services and equipment be accessible and usable by people with disabilities where readily achievable, and directs FCC studies on advanced services for schools and universal service
Protects privacy of customer phone records, requires pay-phone operators be compensated per call, and prohibits carriers from subsidizing competitive services with ratepayer revenue

Requires TV sets 13 inches or larger to include circuitry letting parents block programs by rating, and establishes an internet-service liability shield for providers who restrict objectionable content

analysis.who_pays: The regional Bell companies pay by being forced to lease and interconnect their networks with competitors before they can enter long distance. Long-distance carriers pay by facing Bell entry into their market. Local governments pay through preemption of their authority over telecom franchising and rights-of-way fees, and satellite TV is exempted from local taxes. Consumers bear the risk side of deregulation: weaker cable rate review and easier media consolidation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Bell phone companies, long-distance carriers, local governments

drawbacks.text: It bars the FCC from enforcing most broadcast ownership limits, allowing ownership of stations across TV and other mass media, and sets a national TV audience-reach cap of 35 percent with a study toward loosening it - consolidating media voices into fewer companies

It replaces routine cable rate regulation with a complaint-driven system: the FCC may review a rate increase only if at least ten subscribers or three percent of subscribers file individual complaints within 90 days

It lets Bell companies seek interim authority to sell long-distance service before FCC competition rules are complete, and its competitive safeguards for local markets sunset three years after enactment regardless of whether real competition has arrived

It creates federal criminal penalties for transmitting 'patently offensive' sexual or excretory material to anyone the sender believes is under 18, a speech restriction that raises censorship concerns for online communication
It preempts local regulation of telecom services and bars discriminatory franchise or rights-of-way fees, cutting off a revenue and bargaining tool for local governments

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real competition in the local phone market - genuine potential savings for consumers - in exchange for deregulation of broadcast ownership, cable rates, and Bell entry into new businesses. The competition provisions are the strongest part: mandatory interconnection, unbundling, number portability, and slamming protections address real monopoly power. But the deregulation side is a serious cost: relaxed media ownership rules concentrate control of local news, and complaint-only cable rate review leaves customers with little practical recourse against price increases. The bill is a real bet that competition will discipline prices where regulators no longer do.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 305-117 on August 4, 1995, but the Senate never passed this House bill, and it died when the 104th Congress ended; the telecommunications overhaul reached President Clinton in 1996 through the Senate's own bill instead.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Bliley (R-VA) introduced the Communications Act of 1995 on May 3, 1995, with 25 original co-introducers including Rep. John Dingell (D-MI), and 26 additional cosponsors (8 Democrats, 18 Republicans) followed
The House Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported amended 38-5, and the Judiciary Committee was discharged on July 24, 1995
The Rules Committee structured floor debate under H. Res. 207, and on August 4, 1995 the House adopted a Democratic motion to recommit with instructions 224-199 before passing the bill 305-117
The final vote split mostly by party: 208 of 231 House Republicans voted yes and 97 of 202 House Democrats voted yes, with 98 Democrats voting no
The Senate never passed H.R. 1555, and the bill received no further action before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The House bill itself never became law, but its substance was largely carried into the Telecommunications Act of 1996 through the Senate's version, so the industries it reshaped got nearly everything: Bell companies won a path into long distance, broadcasters won longer licenses and looser ownership caps, and cable operators won lighter rate oversight. The internet-liability and V-chip provisions also became law. Opponents of media consolidation and cable deregulation did not stop them.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was bipartisan in totals (305-117) but split by party underneath: 208 of 231 Republicans voted yes while Democrats split 97-98, and on the Democrats' motion to recommit the alignment was stark, 180 of 202 Democrats in favor against 43 of 231 Republicans.

industries.note: License terms stretch from five to seven years, renewals become largely automatic if the station avoided serious violations, ownership caps on owning stations across media are lifted, and advanced-TV licenses would go first to existing broadcasters. Fewer, larger media companies mean less local news diversity for viewers, and the FCC's power to police concentration shrinks.

They must open their networks to competitors through interconnection, unbundling, and resale, but in exchange gain entry into long-distance, manufacturing, electronic publishing, and video - after state certification of competition, with an interim long-distance entry path available sooner. Customers of their monopoly local service gain the competition mandate, but the safeguards sunset within three years.

Routine rate regulation gives way to a complaint-only review system that takes effect only if ten subscribers or three percent file individual complaints, while telephone companies gain the right to enter their video markets. The rate deregulation runs against subscribers; the new telephone-company competition is the offsetting benefit consumers were promised.

Their protected market opens to the regional Bell companies once those companies certify local competition, with an interim entry path even earlier. The loss to them comes from competition, which is the same force the bill promises consumers.

Interactive computer service providers are exempted from liability for third-party content and for good-faith content filtering, the ancestor of the liability framework internet platforms rely on. But the same bill adds federal criminal penalties for transmitting patently offensive material to minors online.

Bell companies are barred from alarm monitoring for six years and barred from subsidizing pay-phone service with ratepayer revenue, and pay-phone operators must be compensated per call, protecting small independents from being undercut by below-cost Bell pricing.
